title: Common ports and protocols
summary: Learn what ports are, how they let one device run many services at once, and memorise the common port numbers and protocols every helpdesk technician needs.
objectives: Explain what a port number is and why services use them
Tell the difference between TCP and UDP and when each is used
Recall the well-known ports for HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH and RDP
Match common protocols to the tasks they perform
List which ports are open on a machine using the command line
Recognise how a blocked port causes specific service failures

quiz.q: What is a port number used for?
options: Identifying a physical cable socket only
Directing traffic to the right service on a device
quiz.why: A port number lets one IP address run many services at once by directing each connection to the correct application, such as a web server on port 443.

quiz.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
quiz.why: HTTPS, secure web traffic, uses TCP port 443 by default, while plain HTTP uses port 80.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP is wireless, UDP is wired
TCP is reliable and connection-oriented, UDP is fast and connectionless
quiz.why: TCP sets up a connection and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery; UDP is connectionless and faster, used where speed matters more than perfect delivery, like DNS and streaming.

quiz.q: Which protocol and port would you use for a secure remote terminal to a Linux server?
quiz.why: SSH provides an encrypted remote command-line session over TCP port 22; Telnet (port 23) does the same but with no encryption and should be avoided.

quiz.q: Name the default port used by Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).
quiz.why: RDP uses TCP port 3389, the protocol used to remotely control a Windows desktop, which helpdesk teams use constantly.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why does a single server need port numbers at all?
quiz.answer: A server has one IP address but runs many services, so port numbers tell incoming traffic which service it is meant for, like apartment numbers at one street address.
quiz.why: Ports multiplex many services onto one IP, so web, email, and remote access can all share the same machine without confusion.

body_markdown:
## One address, many services

A single device has one **IP address** but often runs many services at once — a web server, an email server, a remote-access service. How does incoming traffic know which one it wants? **Port numbers**. Think of the IP address as a building's street address and the port as the apartment number inside. A port is a 16-bit number from 0 to 65535, and the combination of IP address and port is called a **socket**.

## TCP and UDP

Ports belong to one of two **transport protocols**. **TCP** sets up a connection first and guarantees that data arrives complete and in order — reliable but with a little overhead. **UDP** just fires data off without a handshake — fast and lightweight, but with no delivery guarantee. Web pages and file transfers use **TCP**; DNS lookups, voice calls, and live streaming often use **UDP** because speed matters more than perfect delivery.

## The ports you must know

Certain **well-known ports** (0-1023) come up daily on the helpdesk. Memorise these:

```text
20/21  FTP        file transfer
22     SSH        secure remote terminal
23     Telnet     remote terminal (insecure, avoid)
25     SMTP       sending email
53     DNS        name resolution
67/68  DHCP       automatic addressing
80     HTTP       web (unencrypted)
110    POP3       receiving email
143    IMAP       receiving email (server-side)
443    HTTPS      secure web
3389   RDP        Remote Desktop (Windows)
```

If you only memorise a handful, make them **80, 443, 53, 22, 3389, and 25** — they appear in tickets constantly.

## How ports explain faults

Blocked ports cause very specific symptoms. If web pages on `https://` fail but `http://` works, port **443** may be blocked. If a user cannot reach Remote Desktop, suspect port **3389**. If email sends but does not receive, look at the receiving ports (**110/143**) rather than the sending port (**25**). Matching a symptom to a port number is a core diagnostic skill.

## Seeing ports in action

Windows shows active connections and listening ports with **netstat**:

```bash
netstat -an

Proto  Local Address      Foreign Address     State
TCP    0.0.0.0:443        0.0.0.0:0           LISTENING
TCP    192.168.1.42:50122 93.184.216.34:443   ESTABLISHED
```

The `LISTENING` line means a service is waiting on that port; `ESTABLISHED` means an active connection. You can also test whether a remote port is reachable from PowerShell:

```bash
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
```

## Your task

Write out the protocol and transport type (TCP or UDP) for ports 22, 53, 80, 443, and 3389 from memory. Then run `netstat -an` on your PC and find at least one port in the `LISTENING` state. Finally, use `Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443` and confirm the connection succeeds.

slides.title: Common ports and protocols
slides.narration: Welcome back. So far we've covered addresses and the services that hand them out and resolve names. Today we learn how one device juggles many services at once, using ports, and we'll memorise the protocol port numbers that come up in helpdesk tickets every single day. This is one of the most practical lessons in the whole module.

slides.title: The ports you must know
bullets: 80 HTTP and 443 HTTPS for the web.
53 DNS for name resolution.
22 SSH and 3389 RDP for remote access.
25 SMTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP for email.
slides.code:
22   SSH      443  HTTPS
53   DNS      3389 RDP
80   HTTP     25   SMTP
slides.narration: Now the part to memorise. Eighty is H T T P, plain web traffic. Four forty-three is H T T P S, secure web. Fifty-three is D N S, name resolution. Twenty-two is S S H, a secure remote terminal. Thirty-three eighty-nine is R D P, Windows Remote Desktop, which you'll use constantly. And for email: twenty-five is S M T P for sending, one ten is P O P three and one forty-three is I M A P for receiving.

slides.title: Insecure ports to avoid
bullets: Telnet on 23 sends everything in clear text.
FTP on 20 and 21 is also unencrypted.
Prefer SSH over Telnet, SFTP over FTP.
Seeing these open can be a security flag.
slides.narration: A quick safety note. Some old protocols send everything, including passwords, in clear text. Telnet, on port twenty-three, is the classic example, and you should use S S H on port twenty-two instead. Plain F T P on ports twenty and twenty-one is similarly unencrypted, so prefer secure alternatives. On the job, seeing these legacy ports open can itself be a security red flag worth raising.

slides.title: How ports explain faults
bullets: HTTPS fails but HTTP works: suspect port 443.
Can't reach Remote Desktop: suspect port 3389.
Email sends but won't receive: check 110 or 143.
Match the symptom to the port number.
slides.narration: Here's why this matters for troubleshooting. Blocked ports cause very specific symptoms. If secure web pages fail but plain ones work, port four forty-three might be blocked. If a user can't reach Remote Desktop, suspect thirty-three eighty-nine. If email sends fine but won't receive, look at the receiving ports, one ten and one forty-three, not the sending port. Matching a symptom to a port is a core diagnostic skill.

slides.title: Seeing ports with netstat
bullets: netstat -an lists active connections and ports.
LISTENING means a service is waiting on that port.
ESTABLISHED means an active live connection.
A fast way to see what a machine is doing.
slides.narration: Let's see ports for real. On Windows, net stat dash a n lists active connections and listening ports. A line marked LISTENING means a service is sitting on that port, waiting for connections. A line marked ESTABLISHED means there's an active, live connection right now. It's a quick, powerful way to see exactly what a machine is doing on the network.

slides.title: Testing a remote port
bullets: Test-NetConnection checks a port from PowerShell.
Confirms whether a service is reachable.
Great for proving a firewall is blocking you.
Returns True or False for the port test.
slides.narration: One more handy tool. In PowerShell, Test dash Net Connection lets you check whether a specific port on a remote machine is reachable. Type the host name and dash Port four forty-three, and it tells you true or false. This is brilliant for proving whether a firewall is blocking you, rather than guessing. If it comes back false, the port is closed or filtered somewhere along the path.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Ports route traffic to services on one IP.
TCP is reliable; UDP is fast.
Task: list listening ports and test port 443.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Ports route traffic to the right service on a single I P address. T C P is reliable, U D P is fast. And the ports to know cold are twenty-two, fifty-three, eighty, four forty-three, thirty-three eighty-nine, and twenty-five. Your task: write out the protocol and transport type for ports twenty-two, fifty-three, eighty, four forty-three, and thirty-three eighty-nine from memory. Then run net stat dash a n and find a listening port, and use Test Net Connection to reach port four forty-three. See you next time for network hardware.
